title: Jasper Cole - Backpack Hero - Player Upgrades and Progression
speaker: Jasper Cole
summary: Jasper Cole, lead developer of Backpack Hero, explains how the inventory-management roguelike structures, creates and balances roughly 865 items and handles player progression. He traces the idea to Dicey Dungeons, Slay the Spire and Deus Ex inventories, describes a data-driven 'item2' system of triggers, effects and targets that also enables modding, and lists sources of item ideas: planned needs, community contests, shapes, themes, art-first and exploring the possibility space. Balance comes from rarity, stats, item size, niches, community feedback and analytics. Progression is item-based and flexible, with backpack expansion on level-up and a story-mode town for meta progress.

insights.claim: Backpack Hero differs from other item-collecting roguelikes because players must decide not only which items to carry but how to arrange them spatially in a grid inventory.
insights.detail: Cole describes it as a strategy roguelike where you build something like a deck of items while fighting waves of enemies; the twist is organising and structuring the items within the backpack.
insights.quote: not only are you choosing which items to have with you but you are also having to determine how you organize and structure these items within your inventory

insights.claim: Dicey Dungeons uses ability size in a grid as a cost, with more useful skills taking more space, an idea Backpack Hero builds on along with Deus Ex's inventory where weapons, ammo and utilities compete for space.
insights.detail: Cole spent years trying grid-based variants (placing heroes, placing cards) before inventory management clicked. In Dicey Dungeons placement doesn't matter but size does; in Deus Ex many kinds of items compete for limited inventory, forcing interesting choices about what to bring.
insights.quote: each ability basically has a cost assigned to it which is the size of the ability

insights.claim: Backpack Hero refactored from hand-coded items to an 'item2' system where most items are defined through drop-down menus of trigger, effect, value and target in the Unity inspector, which also enabled mod support.
insights.detail: The original system required manually writing code, so items had to be simple. In item2, the wooden sword is configured as 'on use, damage, 7, selected enemy'. Most of the ~865 items use it, and modders can use the same system.
insights.quote: once we created this item2 system not only did it allow us to create many different items

insights.claim: Items should serve many different functions (consumables, weapons, utility buffs) so the player constantly faces trade-offs like long-term shield versus a meal for the next fight.
insights.detail: Cole cites the water flask (energy consumable), weapons, and a whetstone that buffs adjacent weapons for the combat. Because items aren't all weapons or all consumables, every pickup poses a real question.
insights.quote: Because they have so many different purposes the player is always challenged to make interesting decisions

insights.claim: Backpack Hero generates item ideas from several sources: items planned for a known need, community contests, an item's grid shape, seasonal themes, and art drawn first with mechanics worked out afterwards.
insights.detail: The wooden sword was planned as the simplest starter weapon; the black manastone came from a Discord vote; designers ask 'what about an L-shaped item'; a Halloween set was built to synergise thematically; and the artist drew a sheet of 100 possible items to work backwards from, iterating collaboratively.
insights.quote: allowing them just to draw whatever they want and working backwards from that

insights.claim: With items built from trigger, effect and target lists, designers can look for combinations not yet used and pick one as a creative starting point for an item with no idea attached.
insights.detail: For a rose sprite with no function, Cole reasoned it isn't something you use, so chose a start-of-turn trigger, then an appropriate effect and target. Triggers include on use, each turn, turn end, once per combat and on enemy defeat; effects include damage, block, heal, energy and max health; targets include player, one enemy, all enemies and everyone.
insights.quote: From this possibility space you can it is possible to immediately create item ideas without having an interesting idea going in

insights.claim: Rarity balances items: common items are weaker, broader and fine to find multiples of, while legendary items can be stronger and more complex because players rarely get more than one or two per run.
insights.detail: Cole calls rarity the simplest of Backpack Hero's balance systems because drop rates for each rarity are known.
insights.quote: ideally it is something that the player is not going to find multiple times on their run

insights.claim: In a spatial inventory game, item size is a balance lever alongside stats: smaller items are generally more effective and easier to fit, so resizing an item changes its power.
insights.detail: Cole notes the machete's damage could simply be tuned up or down, but sprites can also be grown from three spaces to four or shrunk to two, creating interesting relationships between items.
insights.quote: smaller items for the most part are more effective in the game, easier to use, and easier to fit in with more items

insights.claim: Avoid items that are strictly better versions of others; give each item a niche so there is always some reason to consider it.
insights.detail: Even though the fox rapier is generally much better than the machete in Backpack Hero, the team tries to ensure you won't always replace one with the other.
insights.quote: we have tried to make it so there aren't items that are just better versions of other items

insights.claim: Balancing hundreds of items needs run analytics (character, items taken and skipped, killers, win/loss), but publicly nerfing items based on analytics drew criticism from players.
insights.detail: Cole says 865 items can't be balanced through conversations with players alone. Backpack Hero got criticism for being overly public about analytics, as some players disliked items being made worse because data showed they were too good.
insights.quote: some people didn't like the idea we would make an item worse because the analytics showed it was too good

insights.claim: Item-based progression is tangible and flexible: unlike permanent level-up choices that lock in a build, an inventory can be reorganised into new loadouts as challenges change.
insights.detail: In Backpack Hero all progression is through items: after each fight there are seven drops to pick from, and you can always see what you have and re-evaluate.
insights.quote: In some games when you level up, you make permanent decisions which lock you into are a certain build type

insights.claim: Backpack Hero's level-up opens new backpack spaces, which Cole considers the best-working part of the game because the progression is visible and fits the collecting theme.
insights.detail: Items are built around space, such as an energy item that is disabled if adjacent to any other item, encouraging players to carve out a corner for it.
insights.quote: Additional spaces open up in your backpack and you are able to expand your backpack. This is probably the part of the game that works the best

insights.claim: Placement-based buffs, like gems that boost adjacent weapons, make power growth visible in the arrangement, which feels more tangible than raising a number on a character sheet.
insights.detail: In Backpack Hero the wooden sword normally deals 7 damage but surrounded by gems it deals 15.
insights.quote: the arrangement makes it feel tangible and fun in a way where just increasing a number on a character sheet can feel a lot more abstract

insights.claim: Backpack Hero's story mode lets players save an item to bring back to town even after losing, using collected items to build and upgrade town structures as meta progress.
insights.detail: Cole says the team doesn't have all the answers yet but considers constant progress across runs, with upgrades and unlocks, an important piece of a modern roguelike.
insights.quote: you are always bringing items back to your town even if you lose

insights.claim: Cole's top advice is to release something: Backpack Hero's free itch.io release and subsequent Kickstarter changed the game's trajectory.
insights.detail: The first version was made in January 2022 and released free on itch.io; the May Kickstarter blew up and made Backpack Hero the team's main focus.
insights.quote: Backpack Hero went to the next level when we released it on itch.io and then did the Kickstarter

insights.claim: Build a wide, flexible possibility space for items early and then explore it fully, so you and modders can create varied loot that makes players interact with the game in fresh ways.
insights.detail: Cole says Backpack Hero had to be recoded because the original item system wasn't flexible enough. He calls varied loot serving multiple purposes the lifeblood of a replayable roguelike, and asks for progression that is both visible and flexible.
insights.quote: it is really important that you create this possibility space where you will be able to create a wide variety of items or power ups within your game
